Cloth that reads on camera

A garment is not finished when it drapes correctly. It is finished when it reads correctly under the light of the shot it lives in. This is the workflow I use to get from a pattern to cloth that survives the render - and the four places it usually fails.

1. The fabric preset is a starting point, not an answer

Silk, cotton, denim and leather presets each carry a weight, a bend and a stretch. Picking the closest one and simulating is how a garment ends up looking like every other garment. What works is choosing the preset nearest the truth and then adjusting the three properties that actually drive the read:

  • Weight decides how fast it falls and how it settles.
  • Bend decides whether a fold is soft or sharp - the single biggest tell.
  • Stretch decides whether seams pull when the character moves.

2. Particle distance is a budget, not a quality dial

Lower particle distance means finer cloth and a longer simulation. The mistake is setting it globally low "to be safe" - that turns a two-minute sim into forty and still produces a garment that clips at the shoulder. Better to keep the distance moderate and pin the problem areas: shoulder seams, underarm, waistband. Pinning costs nothing at render time and removes the artefacts that a global quality bump would not.

3. Wind is a lighting decision disguised as physics

Wind strength and turbulence are usually dialled for "movement". They should be dialled for the shot. A calm interior with a strong breeze looks wrong because the fabric is moving for no reason the camera can see. The rule I follow: if the shot has no visible air, the cloth moves only when the character does.

4. The render pass decides whether it worked

Simulated cloth that looks like paper under a soft key light is the most common failure, and it is not a simulation problem. Cloth needs a specular response - sheen, not gloss - and a normal map with enough high-frequency detail to catch the light at the fold. If the garment reads as flat, fix the material before touching the simulation.

The other half is thickness. Real cloth has an edge, and a single-sided plane catches light wrong at every silhouette. Giving it a small, consistent thickness in the render - not the sim - fixes most edge artefacts for free.

5. Dressed, not simulated

The last step is the one that gets skipped. A perfectly simulated garment on a character in a T-pose reads as a demo. The work is dressing it: posing the character, letting the cloth settle against the body, and only then simulating the action. Garments that are simulated already in motion tend to look like they are being blown, not worn.
